title: Truly subcubic APSP
formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least \(2/3\)? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs \(O(1)\), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on \(O(\log  n)\)-bit index words cost \(O(1)\). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.

progress.text: Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish truly subcubic equivalences between APSP and several path, matrix, and weighted-triangle tasks.
Williams gives a randomized real-RAM algorithm with time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$, demonstrating a substantial subpolynomial saving while leaving a fixed exponent improvement unresolved.

Akmal and Fischer solve the node-weighted zero-triangle problem in matrix-multiplication time; their introduction explicitly distinguishes it from the edge-weighted variant governed by the APSP hypothesis.

references.title: Faster all-pairs shortest paths via circuit complexity

status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is a fixed exponent saving for arbitrary real edge weights; the 2026 node-weighted triangle result does not supply it.

context_blocks.text: Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.

importance.reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.

sentences: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a weighted directed graph.
The graph may contain negative edges but no negative cycle.
The target is an algorithm with a fixed positive improvement over the cubic exponent in the specified comparison-addition model.
Small subpolynomial savings do not meet that target.
The question matters both as a basic graph optimization problem and as the organizing hypothesis behind many conditional running-time lower bounds.
